title: Metadata, Directory Listings, and Exposed Portals
introduction: You have found a PDF on Google. You have not opened it yet. Before you decide whether to view it — and how to handle it professionally — there is already information available about it that does not require reading a single word of the document itself. That information is the metadata: the hidden notes attached to the file that most people never think about.

sections.heading: Document metadata: the hidden profile of every file
sections.content:
Every document file — every PDF, every Word document, every Excel spreadsheet — contains metadata embedded at the time of creation. Metadata is the hidden layer of information about the file itself, separate from the file's actual content.

What document metadata typically contains:

**Author name**: The name registered to the software when the file was created or last edited. This is often a person's real full name, or an internal username.

**Organisation**: The company or department name registered to the software licence.

**Software and version**: The application used to create the file (e.g., 'Microsoft Word 2019', 'Adobe Acrobat Pro 2021', 'LibreOffice 7.5'). Version information reveals the software era — and potentially, whether it was updated.

**Creation and modification dates**: When the file was originally created and when it was last saved. The modification history can reveal when internal drafts were circulated.

**Revision count**: How many times the document was edited before this version was saved. A high revision count on a document marked 'DRAFT' suggests active development.

**Embedded paths**: Some applications embed the local file path where the document was last saved — revealing internal directory structure such as C:\Users\sarah.mitchell\Documents\HR\Confidential\Salaries_2024.xlsx.

This information is completely separate from the document's text content. You can extract it without opening the document, without reading a word of it, and without downloading it in a way that would raise ethical concerns — because metadata extraction tools can read it from a file's header.

callout.title: What metadata reveals in a professional engagement
callout.content:
Author name from a PDF → real employee name → LinkedIn search → current role, team, seniority level → social engineering preparation target.

Software version from a document → the organisation was still using that version as of the document date → vulnerability research for that specific software version.

Embedded file path → internal directory naming conventions → useful when later assessing internal systems.

Organisation name in metadata → confirms which specific division or subsidiary created the document — even if the document doesn't say.

sections.heading: How to extract metadata (the tools professionals use)
sections.content:
You do not need to open a file to read its metadata.

**ExifTool** (free, cross-platform command line tool):
exiftool document.pdf
exiftool *.pdf (processes a batch)
Reads metadata from PDFs, Word documents, images, spreadsheets, and hundreds of other file formats. Shows all embedded fields: author, software, creation date, GPS coordinates (for images), and more.

**PDF metadata online readers**: Multiple free online tools accept a PDF upload and display its metadata — useful for quick checks without a command line.

**Browser developer tools for images**: Images contain EXIF data including camera make, model, GPS coordinates (if location was not stripped), and timestamp. Social media platforms strip this automatically. Images uploaded directly to websites often do not have it stripped.

Professional practice: When a document is found in Google results during an authorised engagement, download it, extract the metadata before opening, and document the findings. Metadata findings belong in the report alongside any content-based findings — they confirm employees, technology stack, and internal naming conventions.

callout.title: The journalist's method and the security parallel
callout.content: Investigative journalists have used document metadata for decades. In 2003, the UK government published a dossier on Iraqi WMDs in Word format. Metadata revealed the document had been edited by multiple people including a named intelligence official — contradicting government claims about its authorship. In 2010, a Word document from a major law firm revealed the names of partners who had reviewed a sensitive filing. In security: the same technique, the same tools, the same information — applied to understanding who produced an internal document and what technology they used.

sections.heading: Directory listings: the open cupboard
sections.content:
A web server's job is to serve files when visitors request them. When a visitor requests a URL that corresponds to a directory — rather than a specific file — the server has two choices:

1. Return a specific file (usually index.html or index.php) — the normal, intended behaviour.
2. Display a list of every file in that directory — the misconfigured behaviour.

Option 2 is called directory listing or directory indexing, and it is a misconfiguration in web server settings (Apache, Nginx, IIS all have it disabled by default — but it can be accidentally enabled).

When directory listing is enabled, visiting /backup/ on a web server displays something like:

```
Index of /backup
[DIR]  2024/               (01-Jul-2024)
[   ]  database_backup.sql.gz  (2.4M)
[   ]  config_prod.tar.gz      (847K)
[   ]  server_logs_june.zip    (12M)
```

Every file is directly downloadable by clicking. The directory is fully navigable. Nothing in this interaction is technically unusual — the server is behaving exactly as configured. The configuration is simply wrong.

The Google Dork that finds this: intitle:"index of"
Combined with a target: site:target.com intitle:"index of"
Added specificity: site:target.com intitle:"index of" inurl:backup

An open directory containing backup files, configuration archives, or log files is a critical finding in every professional penetration test. The backup file likely contains the database. The configuration archive likely contains credentials. The log file likely contains internal IP addresses, usernames, and error messages revealing the technology stack.

callout.title: Professional ethics: documenting vs. downloading
callout.content: Finding an open directory with backup files during an authorised engagement: record the URL, record the filenames visible in the listing, record the file sizes and modification dates. Do NOT download the backup file. A 2.4MB database backup containing customer data is exactly the kind of evidence that creates legal complexity if you download it to your laptop. Document the existence of the exposure. Report it as critical. The client's team is responsible for the remediation and — if necessary — breach assessment. Minimum necessary access is the professional standard: prove the exposure exists, do not exploit it further than the proof requires.

sections.heading: Exposed login portals: the door in the index
sections.content:
An admin login portal is not inherently a vulnerability. Every web application with an admin interface has one. The question is whether it is:

1. Accessible only from internal networks (correct configuration)
2. Accessible from the internet but requires credentials (acceptable, depending on the application)
3. Accessible from the internet, indexed by Google, and potentially running vulnerable software (a finding)

The reconnaissance value of finding an exposed login portal:

**Confirms the technology stack.** The login page design, version numbers in the footer, and URL structure often identify the specific software running (WordPress, Drupal, Jira, Confluence, phpMyAdmin, Tomcat Manager, etc.).

**Reveals version information.** 'Powered by WordPress 5.4' in a page footer is the kind of information that sends a professional directly to CVE databases — WordPress 5.4 has specific known vulnerabilities.

**Identifies the entry point for credential testing.** During the active phase — with explicit authorisation — the login portal is where credential attacks are attempted. Knowing it exists and knowing its exact URL is the prerequisite.

**Common exposed portals found via Google Dorking:**
inurl:wp-admin — WordPress admin
inurl:phpmyadmin — database admin interface
inurl:manager/html — Apache Tomcat Manager
inurl:jira — Atlassian Jira
inurl:confluence — Atlassian Confluence
inurl:/admin/login — generic admin panel

Professional practice: Document the portal URL, capture a screenshot of the login page, note any version information visible, confirm the URL is in scope for active testing, and include in the report as a finding that requires active-phase follow-up.

keyTerms.definition: Structured data embedded within a file that describes the file itself: author, creation date, software used, organisation. Separate from the file's content and extractable without reading the document.
A free, cross-platform command-line tool for reading and writing metadata from hundreds of file types including PDFs, Word documents, images, and spreadsheets.
A standard format for metadata embedded in image files. Can contain camera make, model, settings, and GPS coordinates if location services were enabled when the photo was taken.

A web server configuration that displays the contents of a directory as a browsable file list when no default page exists in that directory. A misconfiguration that exposes all files in the directory.
The professional standard in security testing: gather only the minimum evidence needed to prove a vulnerability exists. Do not download, copy, or exfiltrate data beyond what proves the finding.
